In a thin jacket, at minus ten degrees

January 9th, evening. It’s minus ten degrees at Bucharest airport. Mihai is waiting for Kenji, who is coming from Madrid with a suitcase full of soup base. Ana, six days from her due date, is waiting for them at home.
Kenji! Over here!
Mihai! Long time no see! …Brr, it’s cold! What is this freezing cold?!
It’s minus ten today. I told you on the phone, and you still came in a thin jacket?
My suitcase was full of soup base, so my coat didn’t fit.
Soup before your coat, then. That’s so you.
Of course. I came to make Ramen Hana-chan, after all.
Your plane was a bit late, right?
Yeah. On the plane they announced: “Due to snow in Bucharest, arrival will be delayed by thirty minutes.”
Even though the restaurant is so busy, you came all this way for us. Thank you.
What are you talking about? I promised, didn’t I? That I’d make your ramen.
(Opening the door) Kenji! Welcome! It’s so cold, and you really came!
Ana! Wow, your belly’s grown. The baby could be born any time now.
The due date is the 15th. Six more days.
Right. By then I’ll finish the ramen for the baby. …Ah, the baby can’t eat yet, can it?
(Laughing) So it’s not for the baby, it’s for us.
Exactly. It’s a ramen to help the mum get her strength back. For the time after the birth, I’ll make lots of soup and freeze it in advance.
But our kitchen is small. It’s not even half the size of the one at your restaurant in Madrid.
No problem. Ramen isn’t made with the size of the kitchen. It’s made with the heart.
Kenji, I’ve heard that one before.
(Laughing) …Tomorrow I’ll get up early to go to the market. Mihai, show me the way.
I’m on leave from tomorrow, so sure. …But tomorrow it’ll be minus twelve.
It’s not that I’m going even though it’s cold. It’s precisely because it’s cold that we need ramen!

ta-me-ni: three even syllables, no strong stress. The “e” is short and open, like in “bed”. Don’t confuse it with たまに (tamani, “now and then”).
no-ni: the two syllables stick to the word before: “samuinoni”. When a sentence ends in のに… (いった のに…), the voice drops and stretches a little: that’s how regret sounds.
ma-i-na-su: the final “u” is barely heard (“mainas”). じゅうど has a long “u”: jū-do. Same for じゅうにど (jū-ni-do).
1. ～ために: “in order to…”, “for…” (purpose)

ため means “benefit, purpose”. With に after it, it shows the PURPOSE of the main action. It attaches to verbs in the DICTIONARY form and to nouns with の. It’s English “in order to / so as to” and “for”.
verb (dictionary) + ために
I came to make ramen.
I get up early to go to the market.
noun + の ために
I make soup for the baby.
I freeze it in advance for after the birth.
ため の + noun
ramen for the baby
ため です (at the end)
It’s so I can buy good bones.

に can be dropped (ラーメン を つくる ため きた), but in speech it sounds more natural with に. You’ve already met the form in stories: Mihai wrote in his notebook “to note down what he wanted to tell Ana” (ch. 19), grandpa learned “¡Hola!” “for Ana” (ch. 27).
With people, の ために has a special warmth: きみたち の ために = “for you, for your sake”. Just like in English: “I did it for you”.
2. ～ため(に): “because of…” (cause, formal style)

The same ため can also show CAUSE, especially in announcements, news and official letters. You can tell from the meaning: if the second part is something you don’t control (a delay, a closure), it’s a cause.
noun + の ため
Due to snow, arrival is delayed.
verb (any tense) + ため
Because the road froze, the bus stopped.
い-adj. + ため
Due to the cold, there are few people at the market.
な-adj. + な ため
Because the room was quiet, I slept well.

Compared with から and ので (ch. 29): から is spoken and subjective, ので is polite and “explains”, ため is official and cold, like “due to / owing to” in a press release. Kenji is quoting it from the announcement on the plane; in conversation he’d say ゆき が ふった から、おくれた.

Cause or purpose? Usually: a verb in the PAST or a state (こおった, さむい) → cause. A dictionary-form verb for an action you want (かう, いく) → purpose. ゆき の ため = because of the snow; あかちゃん の ため = for the baby: here the meaning decides.
3. ～のに: “even though…, and yet…”

のに links two REAL facts, where the second goes against expectations. Unlike けど, のに carries a feeling: surprise, annoyance, reproach, regret. English does this with “even though”, “and yet”, “and still”.
Before のに
plain form + のに
I told you on the phone, and yet you came in a thin jacket.

Watch out with な-adjectives and nouns: in the present you use な (not だ): ✗ はじめて だ のに → ✓ はじめて な のに. In the past: はじめて だった のに.
のに can end the sentence, like a sigh: すこし だけ って いった のに! (“And you said just a little!”), きて くれた のに… (“And after he came all this way…”). The second part isn’t said, it’s felt.
After のに you CAN’T put a request, a suggestion or an intention: ✗ さむい のに、いきましょう. Use けど here: ✓ さむい けど、いきましょう. のに describes what HAS happened or what IS, against expectations.

Kenji’s last line plays exactly on this difference: さむい のに いく ん じゃ ない (I’m not going “even though” it’s cold, as if the cold were an obstacle) — さむい から こそ (I’m going PRECISELY because it’s cold).
What you saw in ch. 41 at the end of a line: なおした はず だった のに… = “it should have been fixed… and yet (it isn’t)”. Now you know where the annoyance in Ana’s voice comes from.
5. ために or ように? When ために doesn’t work

ために (purpose) needs two things: the same SUBJECT in both parts and a verb of WILL (an action you choose: つくる, いく, かう). If either condition is missing, Japanese uses ように (you’ll learn it properly later).
✗ Doesn’t work / less common

Rule of thumb: if in English you say “so that I CAN…” or “so that HE…” (another person), think of ように. If you say “in order (for me) to make…”, ために is safe.

はなちゃん ラーメン が できる まで — Until Ramen Hana-chan was ready
On the morning of January 10th, it was minus twelve in Bucharest. Even the window panes were frozen white.
From today, Mihai is on leave for a month. Yesterday morning he had also finished, just in time, the translation of the manual.
Kenji is staying at a small hotel near the Botanical Garden. It’s a five-minute walk to Ana and Mihai’s home.
But that morning, too, Kenji came in the same thin jacket as the day before.
“Kenji, you can’t go to the market dressed like that!” said Ana.
Just then, Mrs Doina from next door opened her door and wrapped her own red scarf around Kenji’s neck.
Mr Petre from the floor above came down too, with an old fur hat.
“It would be a shame if the Japanese chef caught a cold in Romania,” said Mrs Doina.
Seeing Kenji in the big hat and the red scarf, Ana couldn’t help laughing. “You look just like a grandpa from the countryside.”
Mihai and Kenji took the tram to Obor market to buy the ingredients for the soup.
Even though it was so cold, the market was full of people.
Kenji spent a long time choosing bones in front of the butcher’s. “To make a good soup, good bones are the most important thing.”
When Mihai said, “He’s Japanese, and he came from Madrid just to make ramen,” the butcher’s eyes went wide.
And he put three of his best bones in a bag for them, for free. “It’s for the baby. Take them.”
Before leaving the market, Kenji also bought himself some thick gloves.
On the tram home, Kenji held the bag of bones in his arms like a treasure.
As soon as they got home, Kenji started making the noodles right away.
But Romanian flour is a little different from Japanese flour.
To make good noodles, Kenji changed the amount of water little by little and tried again and again.
The first batch of noodles came out too soft, the second too hard.
“In Madrid I can make them with my eyes closed, and here…” said Kenji, frustrated.
Carmen and Kenji could talk in Spanish, so they quickly became friends.
Carmen tasted the third batch and said: “¡Perfecto!”
Kenji breathed a sigh of relief and laughed: “A mother’s tongue doesn’t lie.”
The next day, the soup simmered gently for twelve hours over a low flame. The kitchen window turned white with steam.
The lovely smell spread from the hallway all the way to the stairs.
Towards evening, Mr Petre’s dog sat down in front of the door and wouldn’t budge.
“I’m so sorry. He never usually does this,” Mr Petre apologised, red in the face.
Kenji laughed and gave the dog a soup bone too.
In the evening, Ioana came over to help as well.
To cut the spring onions, Ioana learned from Kenji how to hold the knife.
“Your Japanese is good, Ioana. And you’ve never even been to Japan.” When Kenji praised her like that, Ioana blushed with joy.
Late at night, after everyone else had gone to bed, Mihai and Kenji were alone in the kitchen, keeping an eye on the soup.
“Kenji, thank you, truly. You even closed your restaurant to come for us.”
Stirring the soup, Kenji said quietly: “Do you remember the day you first came to my restaurant?”
“You were alone, and you had a Japanese textbook with you. You looked like you hadn’t come to eat ramen, but to use your Japanese.”
“You couldn’t even say ‘itadakimasu’ properly yet, and still you came every week. And that same Mihai is about to become a dad. Ramen? I’ll make you as many bowls as you want.”
Mihai couldn’t say anything and rubbed his eyes. “I’m copying you. I just got steam in my eyes.”
Kenji laughed and patted him on the shoulder.
On the evening of the 12th, Ramen Hana-chan was finally ready.
Elena, Carmen and Mrs Doina gathered around the table.
On top of every bowl were carrots cut into flower shapes and pink naruto.
“Because Rosa and Sakura are both flowers,” said Kenji.
Ana had said, “Just a little, I had a snack a moment ago,” and yet she drank the soup to the very last drop.
“And you said just a little!” laughed Mihai, and Ana stroked her belly: “It wasn’t me, she wanted to drink it.”
Elena, even though she can’t use chopsticks, ate the noodles with a fork, giving it her all, and even asked for seconds.
Mrs Doina said, “I’ve never had such a delicious soup in my life!” and suggested to Kenji that they swap: this recipe for her sarmale recipe.
Kenji divided the leftover soup into small bags and put it in the freezer.
“For after the birth, I’ve made thirty portions in advance. Even when I go back to Madrid, you’ll be covered with this.”
The freezer filled up with soup, and Mihai’s ice cream no longer fit.
Kenji’s flight home is on the 20th. “Before then, I’d really love to meet Hana-chan.”
That evening, Kenji showed the ramen to Sakura in Hiroshima on a video call.
“It’s the ramen with the name I chose! …But that’s not fair! And I can’t eat it!”
Kenji promised her: “In the summer holidays I’ll make it for you in Hiroshima.”
On the screen, Haruka was laughing too. “To eat that ramen, Sakura will probably be good until summer.”
Before going to bed, Ana looked at the snow outside the window and talked to her belly.
“Hana-chan, the ramen is waiting for you. It’s so very cold, and yet everyone has gathered here for you.”
Inside her belly, a little foot moved, thump. As if it were answering: “I’m coming soon.”
